title: How Architects Solve Common Problems in Older Westchester Homes
excerpt: Older homes in Westchester have character, but they also have quirks. Here's how working with a licensed architect and general contractor can turn those challenges into opportunities.
content:
If you own an older home anywhere in Westchester County, you know the feeling. You love the bones of the place. The craftsmanship. The layout that actually makes sense. But then you open a closet and realize there's barely enough room for a winter coat. The kitchen hasn't been updated since 1987. The bathrooms are cramped. And don't get started on trying to add natural light without tearing down a load-bearing wall.

The good news is that these aren't unsolvable problems. They're just problems that need the right person to solve them. That person is usually a licensed architect in Westchester, NY who understands what makes older homes tick and how to work with their limitations instead of against them.

Load-Bearing Walls and Open Concepts

The biggest roadblock in older homes is simple: people want open-concept living, but the house was built with walls that hold everything up. You can't just grab a sledgehammer and start swinging.

This is where a licensed architect who also works as a general contractor makes a real difference. Silvio Luca, the principal at House Architecture and Construction, runs every project personally. He's both a licensed New York architect and a licensed general contractor. That means he knows how to evaluate which walls can come down, what kind of support is needed if they do, and how to actually execute the work once plans are drawn.

We've done open-concept conversions in homes throughout Westchester, from Scarsdale to Mamaroneck to Rye. The approach is always the same: figure out what the house is actually doing structurally, then design a solution that works with the existing framing instead of fighting it. Sometimes that means a beam. Sometimes it means relocating a wall a few feet. Sometimes it means keeping more walls than you'd initially hoped, but configuring the space so it feels open anyway.

Second Stories and Additions That Fit

A lot of homeowners in Westchester think the only way to get more space is to move. But a second-story addition or home addition in Westchester can often be the better answer. The catch is that it has to look right. An addition that looks like it was bolted on by a contractor who didn't care will haunt you forever.

When we design a second story in Bronxville or Larchmont or Hastings-on-Hudson, we're thinking about the proportions of the original house. The pitch of the roof. The window placement. The materials. The goal is to make it look like it was always meant to be there. That takes architectural thinking. It can't be a cookie-cutter approach.

Permits, Code, and Getting It Right the First Time

Westchester County has multiple municipalities, and each one has its own building department and permit process. That's just how it is. Whether you're in White Plains, Pelham, Tuckahoe, or Ossining, you'll need to work through local requirements. A design-build firm in Westchester that handles both the architectural design and the construction coordination can cut through the back-and-forth.

When Silvio designs a project, he's already thinking about what the building department will ask for. He knows the local inspectors. He knows what documentation they need. He pulls permits himself. This isn't about gaming the system. It's about doing the work right from the start so there are no surprises during construction.
